parts.note: Your tailnet keeps it private, and plain HTTP is fine there. HTTPS (Tailscale Serve) is optional.

guides.fieldsNote: Each person pastes their own token (it starts with ops_) in Settings › Your accounts › 1Password; the app seals it on their device to every machine. Test there lists the vaults it reads.

parts.note: Agents run as you on their machine: they reach your files, gh and ssh, and could read what fleetd's 1Password service account reads. Keep only the logins agents sign in with and the card a Navi buys with in this vault, and nothing else of yours.
parts.title: Make a vault for fleetd

values.label: In it
values.value: Each login agents sign in with, with its website, and the card a project buys with

parts.note: A card in the vault is one an agent on a machine could read. A virtual card with a monthly limit, or a card with a low limit, caps what that could cost.

values.label: Card
values.value: A virtual card with a monthly limit, or a low-limit card: never your main card

parts.note: 1Password can't change a service account's vaults once it's made: for one that reads more, make a new one, paste its token, and revoke the old one on Your service accounts.
parts.title: Make a service account that reads only that vault

values.label: Vaults
values.value: Only fleetd's vault, with read access

guides.test: Test your own token on a machine holding it, then read each person's last Test: one vault each. The first Test on a machine can take up to 4 minutes while its node installs the 1Password SDK
guides.title: 1Password
guides.why: Agents sign in and buy with the logins and card fleetd's service account reads: keep it to one vault of its own.

parts.note: The invite is a link and a code, for one person, good for 7 days. Send it to them yourself.
parts.title: Invite someone

guides.title: Invite people
guides.why: Each person gets their own sign-in, chats and projects; you choose who is an admin.

parts.note: In Terminal on the Mac, in the account it joins from (yours is fine). Xcode itself comes from the App Store, and an iOS simulator runtime with xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS. Without Xcode yet, the Mac still joins: only iOS simulators wait, and its Xcode check says what to do. CocoaPods (for pod install and expo prebuild) comes from Homebrew: brew install cocoapods; its tools check gives the exact line, Homebrew's own install first where there is none.
parts.title: Xcode, once

values.label: In Terminal on the Mac
values.note: Each line says why. It never pipes anything from the network into sudo.
values.value:
# Xcode's licence and its system components, which only an admin can accept and install. Skipped while no Xcode is
# selected yet: setup's Xcode check then says the one command that installs or selects it.
d="$(xcode-select -p 2>/dev/null)" && test -x "$d/usr/bin/xcodebuild" && sudo xcodebuild -license accept && sudo xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch
# Simulators and debugging with no password prompt, for this account.
sudo DevToolsSecurity -enable
sudo dseditgroup -o edit -a "$(id -un)" -t user _developer

parts.note: Paste the join line in Terminal on the Mac, logged in at its screen: launchd runs the node only inside that login, so su and ssh won't do. It installs fleetd for that account and joins as the agents' Mac: a tool every project's agents use, which runs no claude and no Navi and takes no secret. Settings › Hub › Machines › Add machine › A Mac for agents makes the line with its one-time code; if this Mac runs fleetd already, give it that machine's name, and the line replaces it. After a restart, log that account in again: with FileVault on, macOS logs no one in by itself.
parts.title: Join, at the Mac's screen

values.label: In Terminal, logged in at the Mac's screen
values.note: Or on the hub: fleetd pair --worker mac, then add --mac to the line it prints.

parts.note: Turn on fleetd in Accessibility and in Screen Recording, so agents can drive the Mac's apps and you can watch them. The join opens each pane and waits for it, and the node restarts itself within seconds to take up each grant. macOS may ask for an administrator's name and password: type it in that System Settings dialog at the Mac itself, never through fleetd's view of its screen. macOS asks again from time to time; the check says when.
parts.title: Two clicks at the Mac

values.label: Accessibility, at the Mac
values.note: In Terminal there: it opens the pane. Turn on fleetd there.

parts.note: Give the join line the name it has, in the same account, and it becomes the agents' Mac in place, keeping its history. Let the agents running there finish (or stop them) first. Joined under another name or from another account, the old machine stays until you remove it: the Mac's checks say so, and how.
parts.title: A Mac that runs fleetd already

values.label: On the hub, for an old machine of another name
values.note: Where it ran in another account on the Mac, stop it there too: launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/sh.fleetd.node

parts.note: Agents act as the account the node runs in, so they can read what it can. To keep them out of yours, make a standard user for them, log in as it at the Mac's screen, and join from there instead.
parts.title: Optional: a user of its own for agents

values.label: In your own (admin) account's Terminal
values.note: sysadminctl asks for the new user's password, which you keep; agents never get it.
values.value:
# A standard user of its own for agents. You choose its password and keep it.
sudo sysadminctl -addUser agents -fullName "fleetd agents" -password -
sudo dseditgroup -o edit -a agents -t user _developer
# Your own home closed to other users, agents included.
chmod 700 ~

guides.test: Read the Mac's checks, which its node runs every 30 seconds (its grants every 2 while one is off)
guides.title: A Mac for agents
guides.why: Agents on every machine build, test and drive iOS simulators on one Mac: a tool, never a runner, joined from the account at its screen.
